CHAPTER 2: JESUS AND HIS MESSAGE IN CONTEMPORARY CULTURE (Section B: Christianity - Origins and Contemporary Expressions)

BIG IDEA
- Each generation creates its own images of Jesus and expresses meaning in different ways.
- The chapter looks at images of Jesus in contemporary art, film, literature and music, and asks how each image is an inspiration and is relevant to today's culture and society.
- The social, political and historical context of the time affects the image of Jesus that is portrayed.

KEY TERMS
- Contemporary culture: the way of life, values and images of today's society.
- Counter-cultural: going against the main values of the surrounding culture. The message of Jesus is very counter-cultural today.
- Inspiration: something that moves or encourages people to think, feel or act in a new or better way.
- Suffering saviour: an image of Jesus as the one who takes away our sins through his suffering on the cross (the image in The Passion of the Christ).
- Christ-figure: a character in a film (or story) who "mirrors" the life of Jesus, even if the film is not about Jesus.
- Consumerism: a way of life centred on buying and owning things.

OPENING QUOTE - MARCUS J. BORG
- The founders of the world's other major religions lived long lives and were active for decades.
- It is exceptional that so much came from Jesus' brief life; he must have been remarkable.
- His followers are said to have exclaimed: "What manner of man is this?"

CONTEMPORARY CULTURE
- Today's culture has a "frenzy of images" of how to live; people are bombarded and seduced by messages about what gives meaning.
- Glossy magazines and TV ads promise fulfilment, eternal youth, beauty, power and ultimate happiness.
- Society is dominated by consumerism; for many the shopping centre has become the place of worship (they gather on Sunday, listen to music, meet friends, go home happy).
- Within this, the gospel of Jesus strives to be heard; it too offers a vision of how to live and offers meaning.
- Not since its infancy has the message of Jesus been so counter-cultural.
- The world is often marked by greed, superficiality, success, dominance and violence.
- Jesus represents selfless love, service, justice, equality and peace.
- Choosing gospel values today is a demanding choice.

JESUS IN CONTEMPORARY ART
- Artists have been the most significant group in helping us form our image of Jesus.
- A picture is more powerful than words; it reaches our imagination in a way words cannot.
- 1999: the US publication The National Catholic Reporter sponsored a competition to see how artists saw Jesus.
- The editor, Michael Farrell, wanted to see if Jesus still interested artists as the new millennium approached.
- 1,678 entries from nineteen countries.
- The judge was Sister Wendy Beckett, a well-known art expert.
- Winner: "Jesus of the People" by American artist Janet McKenzie (also called "Jesus 2000").
- Farrell said it was controversial: the first thing people noticed was that Jesus was black; the artist also used a young woman as model.
- The painting is realistic or representational.
- Farrell: the point was not what they were looking for but what artists imagined.
- Meaning/relevance: it challenges the idea that Jesus, and ultimately God, belongs to any one ethnic group or gender.
- In a multicultural and multi-faith society, it suggests Jesus came to save us all and should be accessible to all creeds and cultures.

IMAGES OF JESUS IN FILM - OVERVIEW
- Three films from different decades:
- Jesus of Nazareth (1977), directed by Franco Zeffirelli.
- Jesus of Montreal (1989), directed by Denys Arcand.
- The Passion of the Christ (2004), directed by Mel Gibson.
- Social, political and historical context affects the image of Jesus.
- Each film is very different; no one film says all there is to say about Jesus; each director focuses on one dimension.
- Some viewers identify with one more than another; looking at many images, even ones that make us uneasy, helps us develop our own image of Jesus.

JESUS OF NAZARETH (1977) - FRANCO ZEFFIRELLI
- Made for television; broadcast in the Easter season of 1977, in two parts, a little over six and a half hours long.
- Aim: a comprehensive view of the life, death and resurrection of Jesus.
- Begins with Jesus' heroic birth and the dramatic events leading up to it.
- The young Jesus: a special child with piercing blue eyes who seems to know his purpose and mission from a young age.
- Example: the boy Jesus preaching in the temple; he tells his parents, "I am about my father's business."
- Zeffirelli highlights self-knowledge and self-assurance; this continues in the adult Jesus.
- The adult Jesus is serious and in control, with few if any doubts about his role.
- He shows great concern for the oppressed and speaks out for the poor, prostitutes, tax collectors and women in a judgemental culture.
- Jesus is preacher, teacher, miracle worker, forgiver of sins and, above all, one who understands himself as the Messiah.
- Portrays Jesus as a mythical figure: traces his mission from birth to fulfilment, stressing the spiritual and heroic triumph of Jesus the Saviour.
- Context: made when hero myths were back in fashion, like Star Wars and Close Encounters of the Third Kind, which stressed the hero's journey to self-fulfilment.
- A time of growing interest in self-development and making a personal journey; the film offered a unique and inspiring example of a heroic personal journey.
- Image: the heroic, self-assured Saviour / Messiah.

JESUS OF MONTREAL (1989) - DENYS ARCAND
- Made twelve years after Jesus of Nazareth; very different approach.
- Made and set in Montreal, Canada; in French with English subtitles.
- Nominated for an Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film in 1989.
- Plot: a group of actors rework an older play about the life and death of Jesus, written thirty years before by a priest, Father Leclerc.
- Focus on Daniel, the actor who plays Jesus. Daniel's life begins to mirror Jesus' life and he becomes more Christ-like.
- Daniel tries to understand and express what Jesus means for the modern Christian and offers a fresh understanding - but he suffers for this, as Jesus suffered when he challenged the religious leaders.
- Image: Jesus as one who struggles to do what is right and suffers at the hands of the powerful.
- The new play is a huge success with the audience, but Church authorities dislike it and want it stopped.
- Daniel is pressured by religious and civil authorities to stop, but the people want it to go on.
- During the final performance Daniel has an accident that leads to his death.
- After his death, as with Jesus, people who knew him wanted to tell his story and interpret what his death means.
- Daniel found that Jesus' message was one of hope for the people of first-century Palestine: love and right action, respect and sharing.
- This message was seen as inspiring and relevant to the secularised world of the late twentieth century.
- The film looks at the difficulty of telling the story of Jesus in a culture cut off from a sense of the sacred.
- It asks deep questions about who Jesus is and his influence in our lives, and critiques many aspects of modern Western culture.

THE PASSION OF THE CHRIST (2004) - MEL GIBSON
- Released in Ireland on 12 March 2004; astounded audiences on both sides of the Atlantic.
- Raised many questions; brought the contemporary image of Jesus right up to date.
- The image of Jesus is very traditional.
- Focuses on the final twelve hours of Jesus' life; carries explicit warnings about disturbing violence.
- Gibson made it after eighteen years of neglecting his Catholic faith, when he was suddenly struck by a strong sense that he was personally saved by Jesus Christ.
- Image: a suffering saviour - Jesus took away our sins through his suffering on the cross.
- Some accused the film of being anti-Semitic in its portrayal of the Jewish role in Jesus' death.
- Gibson used sources other than scripture for several scenes.
- Aim: to remind Christians of the central message of their faith - Christ suffered and died for their sins.
- Many Christians who had lost sight of this found it inspirational.
- Criticism: it focuses mainly on the passion and gives only brief attention to the resurrection. For many Christians the passion and resurrection are intimately connected - we can only fully understand Christ's suffering in relation to the resurrection.

THE CHRIST-FIGURE IN FILMS
- Images of Jesus are not only in films about his life; characters who "mirror" Jesus appear in unusual films.
- These films are a rich source of insight into our understanding of Jesus.
- Features of Christ-figures:
- Usually outsiders, even from another planet - Superman (Superman: The Movie), E.T. (E.T.: The Extra-Terrestrial), Prot (K-Pax).
- May be surrounded by a number of followers.
- May begin their "work" at the age of thirty.
- One close follower betrays them.
- May "die" and then come back to life.
- May physically resemble or dress like Christ at some point.
- Scholar Anton Karl Kozlovic wrote about Christ-figures in detail, in films such as E.T., Superman: The Movie, K-Pax, The Matrix, The Day the Earth Stood Still and Twelve Monkeys.

JESUS IN CONTEMPORARY LITERATURE - SOPHIE'S WORLD
- Novel by Jostein Gaarder. A young girl, Sophie, does a correspondence course with a mysterious stranger and learns about philosophy and religion.
- Her teacher compares Jesus and Socrates. People have asked "Why did Socrates have to die?" for 2400 years.
- Parallels between Jesus and Socrates:
- Both were enigmatic (mysterious) personalities, even to people of their own time.
- Neither wrote down their teachings; we rely on the picture from their disciples.
- Both were masters of the art of discourse (speaking/debating).
- Both spoke with a self-assuredness that could fascinate as well as exasperate.
- Both believed they spoke on behalf of something greater than themselves.
- Both challenged the power of the community by criticising all injustice and corruption.
- Their activities cost them their lives.
- Both could have saved themselves at their trials by appealing for mercy, but felt their mission would be betrayed unless they kept faith to the bitter end.
- By meeting death bravely they gained an enormous following even after death.
- The teacher does not say they were alike, but that both had a message inseparably linked to their personal courage.
- Image: Jesus as a courageous teacher who died for his convictions.

JESUS IN CONTEMPORARY MUSIC - "NO RELIGION" BY VAN MORRISON
- Looks at the role religion plays in modern life.
- No explicit mention of Jesus, but refers to a "saviour" and to sayings of Jesus: "love your neighbour" and "turn the other cheek".
- Key lyrics: "the whole world has gone astray / That's why there's no religion... here today".
- "It's a choice between fact and fiction."
- Love: "Some say it's unconditional / Other people just remain in doubt".
- Hate is "just the other side of love"; some people want to give their enemies what they think they deserve.
- "Some say why don't you love your neighbours / Go ahead, turn the other cheek / But there's nobody on this planet that can ever be so meek."
- "I can't bleed for you / You have to do it your own way."
- "It's so cruel to expect the saviour to save the day."
- "There's no mystery, and there's nothing hidden."
- The song suggests the teachings of Jesus seem too demanding for people today and that people cannot rely on a saviour; it is largely pessimistic about the place of religion in the modern world.

HOW TO ANSWER EXAM QUESTIONS ON THIS CHAPTER
- Name the image (artist/director/writer, title, date).
- Describe the image of Jesus it presents (e.g. heroic Messiah, suffering saviour, one who suffers at the hands of the powerful, inclusive Jesus of all peoples, courageous teacher).
- Explain its inspiration and its relevance for contemporary culture and society (e.g. multicultural society, secularised world, consumerism, self-development).
- Compare images from different decades to show how context shapes the image of Jesus.

rows.prompt: Describe an image of Jesus found in contemporary art and explain its relevance for contemporary culture and society.
rows.model_answer:
In 1999 the US publication The National Catholic Reporter held a competition to see how artists imagined Jesus as the new millennium approached. It received 1,678 entries from nineteen countries. The winner, chosen by art expert Sister Wendy Beckett, was 'Jesus of the People' by the American artist Janet McKenzie.

The painting is realistic or representational. It was controversial because Jesus is shown as a black person, and the artist used a young woman as her model. The editor, Michael Farrell, said the point was not what they were looking for but what artists imagined.

This image is relevant to today because it challenges the idea that Jesus, and ultimately God, belongs to any one ethnic group or gender. We now live in a multicultural and multi-faith society. The painting suggests that Jesus came to save everyone and should be accessible to all creeds and cultures. It inspires people to see Jesus as one of 'the people' - all people - rather than someone who looks like only one group.
rows.marking_scheme: Description of image 5 marks (artist, title, details) + relevance 5 marks. Very good 8-10, good 5-7, fair 0-4. May refer to: National Catholic Reporter 1999; 1,678 entries, 19 countries; Sister Wendy Beckett; Janet McKenzie; black Jesus; female model; realistic; not the preserve of one ethnic group or gender; multicultural, multi-faith society; Jesus for all.

rows.prompt: Compare the images of Jesus presented in two films you have studied. In your answer, refer to how the context of each film influenced its image of Jesus.
rows.model_answer:
Zeffirelli's 'Jesus of Nazareth' was made for television and shown at Easter 1977. It gives a comprehensive view of Jesus' life, death and resurrection, starting with his heroic birth. The young Jesus has piercing blue eyes and seems to know his mission; in the temple he says 'I am about my father's business.' The adult Jesus is serious, in control, a teacher, miracle worker and forgiver of sins who speaks out for the poor, prostitutes, tax collectors and women, and knows he is the Messiah. It is a mythical image of the heroic Saviour. The context was the return of hero myths like Star Wars and Close Encounters of the Third Kind, and a growing interest in self-development and the personal journey.

Arcand's 'Jesus of Montreal' (1989), in French, is very different. Actors rework Father Leclerc's old play about Jesus. Daniel, who plays Jesus, becomes Christ-like and offers a fresh understanding of Jesus, but the Church and civil authorities want the play stopped. He dies after an accident during the final performance. Jesus is shown as one who struggles to do right and suffers at the hands of the powerful. Its context was the secularised late twentieth century, a culture cut off from the sacred, and the film critiques modern Western culture.

So Zeffirelli's Jesus is confident and triumphant, while Arcand's is struggling and suffering, showing how context shapes each image.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. Two films x (image of Jesus + context) with a comparison. May refer to: Zeffirelli 1977, TV, Easter, temple scene, self-assurance, Messiah, mythical hero, Star Wars era; Arcand 1989, Montreal, French, Father Leclerc, Daniel, suffering at hands of powerful, secularised world, critique of Western culture; Gibson 2004, final 12 hours, suffering saviour, traditional, anti-Semitism claim, little on resurrection.

rows.prompt: Discuss an image of Jesus found in contemporary literature or music, and evaluate its inspiration and relevance for people today.
rows.model_answer:
In the novel 'Sophie's World' by Jostein Gaarder, a young girl takes a correspondence course in philosophy and religion with a mysterious stranger. Her teacher compares Jesus with Socrates. Both were enigmatic personalities, even to people of their own time. Neither wrote down their teachings, so we depend on their disciples. Both were masters of discourse who spoke with a self-assuredness that could fascinate or exasperate, and both believed they spoke on behalf of something greater than themselves. They challenged the power of the community by criticising all injustice and corruption, and this cost them their lives. At their trials both could have saved themselves by appealing for mercy, but they kept faith to the bitter end. By dying bravely they gained a huge following.

The image is of Jesus as a courageous teacher whose message was inseparably linked to his personal courage. This is inspiring today because people are bombarded by messages promising happiness through consumerism, beauty and power. Jesus shows that standing up against injustice and corruption, even at great personal cost, gives life meaning. It is relevant to young people who must make the demanding choice to live gospel values in a world marked by greed and dominance.

In contrast, Van Morrison's 'No Religion' suggests people find Jesus' teachings - 'love your neighbour', 'turn the other cheek' - too hard, showing the challenge of his message today.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. Description of image (8) + inspiration/relevance (8) + evaluation (4). May refer to: Sophie's World, Gaarder, Jesus and Socrates parallels (enigmatic, no writings, discourse, self-assurance, something greater, criticised injustice, died, did not plead for mercy, following after death, courage); or No Religion, Van Morrison, saviour, love your neighbour, turn the other cheek, 'nobody so meek', pessimism; link to contemporary culture and consumerism.

rows.prompt: Outline the main features of a 'Christ-figure' in film and explain what such films can tell us about Jesus.
rows.model_answer:
Images of Jesus in film are not limited to films about his life. Characters that 'mirror' Jesus' life appear in many films, some quite unusual. These Christ-figures are usually outsiders, sometimes even from another planet, such as Superman in Superman: The Movie, E.T. in E.T.: The Extra-Terrestrial and Prot in K-Pax. They may be surrounded by followers and may begin their work at the age of thirty. One of their close followers will betray them. They may 'die' and come back to life, and they may even look or dress like Christ at some point in the film. The scholar Anton Karl Kozlovic has written about this in films like The Matrix, The Day the Earth Stood Still and Twelve Monkeys.

Such films are a rich source of insight into our understanding of Jesus. They show that the story of Jesus - an outsider who comes to help, is betrayed, dies and rises - still shapes the stories our culture tells, even when people are not religious. They indirectly present Jesus as a saviour who gives himself for others.
rows.marking_scheme: Features 6 marks (2 marks each for any three) + explanation 4 marks. May refer to: outsiders/other planet; Superman, E.T., Prot in K-Pax; followers; begin work at thirty; betrayal; death and return; resemble Christ; Kozlovic; The Matrix, The Day the Earth Stood Still, Twelve Monkeys; films a rich source of insight; saviour image.
